doc.title: James Moody — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Howell Epps shows him the C scale
summary: A neighbourhood boy with a saxophone, Howell Epps, taught him a scale; Moody had no formal training.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: And then there was a guy by the name of Howell Epps [phonetic sp.] and he showed me how to play the scale, [scatting] you know. I played that. And then, like, a couple years later, I was drafted in the Air Force. All right? And.
Oh, let me just ask you about -­
Okay. Uh-huh. [affirmative]
Howell Epps. Was he somebody you were in school with or a teacher?
No. He was just a guy that had a saxophone, too. He had one and he had one longer than me.
[laughs]
Like he didn't play. I haven't heard of Howell Epps since then.
And he was somebody you knew in high school?
In Newark. No -­
No? It -- .

-- no. It was just in Newark. We didn't go to the same school. You see, if I was walking down the street anywhere and I heard a saxophone playing out a window, I'd go knock on the door. I mean, in those days, it was funny. People did things like that, you know. But Howell Epps was just a guy that lived in the neighborhood and he had a saxophone. You know, and so.
And he showed you, kind of, the.

Yes, he showed me that, it was just C scale. Now, I know what it was, you know. [laughs] 'Cause I never will forget someone looked at me says, "What are these for?" I said, "I don't know. I don't use those." [laughter]
Those were some of the keys -­
Yes.
-- on the saxophone? [laughter]
Yeah. That was very funny, you know.
So you didn't really have the opportunity to have formal musical training when you were
growing up?
No. No. So, later on, then.
